name: Haraldshaugen
label: Haraldshaugen
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Krosshaugen' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Krosshaugen' (node/1482611036): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/134938214: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Haraldstøtta' (100 m across).
notes: National monument for the 1000th anniversary of the unification of Norway.

text.description:
Haraldshaugen is Norway's national monument to King Harald Fairhair, set on a grassy mound in the northern suburbs of Haugesund. A 17 m granite obelisk stands on top, with four bronze panels around its base showing scenes from the king's life. The mound is ringed by memorial stones, including 29 smaller ones, one for each of the historic counties of Norway. It was unveiled on 18 July 1872, marking a thousand years since the Battle of Hafrsfjord, and the architect was Christian Christie. Tradition says Harald is buried here, but there is no clear archaeological proof.

For a phone photo, the best idea is to start with the old stone cross on the small hill, Krosshaugen, just south of the monument. It is roughly 1,000 years old, and it gives you something close and characterful for the foreground, with the obelisk behind. The wider view over the area includes houses and industry, so the cross and the monument together usually make a stronger picture than a general panorama. Once you have that shot, walk up to the mound for the obelisk itself against the sound and the coast.
text.geographic_location: Haraldshaugen is in the northern suburbs of Haugesund, on the coast about 2 km north of the town centre. Krosshaugen is the small hill just south of the monument.
text.directions_text: From the centre of Haugesund, head north to the northern suburbs; the monument is about 2 km away on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the cross with the monument behind it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole mound and obelisk, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the obelisk closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (south of the national monument, on the small hill beside it). The roughly 1000-year-old stone cross in the foreground, with the monument and the town in the background. From here the old stone cross is in the foreground, and the obelisk rises behind it to the north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the cross on one side of the frame and let the obelisk rise behind it, using the gridlines to keep the upright lines straight. Crouching a little lowers the viewpoint and makes the cross stand out more against the sky. For a second picture, walk up to Haraldshaugen itself and frame the 17 m obelisk against the sound and the coast.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the cross to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the sky keeps its colour and the grey stone does not turn flat. If the sky is bright, tap on the stone, then check the sky has not washed out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: No particular time is needed. Low sun early or late in the day tends to bring out the carving on the stone and the texture of the granite.

text.access_note: This is an outdoor monument site on a hill, reachable on foot and free to visit; check the official site before you go in case of any restrictions.
claims_not_in_sources: Crouching low makes the foreground cross look larger against the obelisk.
Low sun early or late in the day tends to bring out the texture of stone.

name: Haugesund Art Gallery
label: Haugesund Art Gallery
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/447291771: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Haugesund billedgalleri' (75 m across).
notes: The town's art museum in the Skåre district.

text.description: Haugesund Art Gallery (Haugesund Billedgalleri) sits in the north part of the city, looking over the city park and rose garden. It is a good stop if you like buildings that have grown over time. The museum was built in three stages. The oldest part is a house from around 1915, built as a home for Lars and Inga Meling. The main building followed in 1978, designed by the architect David Sandved, and a further extension was added in 2004. Together they cover about 2,210 square metres, with around 1,000 square metres given over to exhibitions. For a photo, that mix of older house and later additions gives you something to look at beyond a single façade. The green setting of the park and rose garden gives you a natural backdrop, and in the growing season you may find flowers to use in the foreground. The gallery's roots go back to the Haugesund Art Society, founded in 1913, and the museum became a municipal institution in 1973. Its collection includes Norwegian and international names such as Edvard Munch, Pablo Picasso and Lars Hertervig, with a strong showing of Western Norway artists. You do not need to go inside to get a good picture. Stay outside, keep your phone level, and take one wide view of the whole group of buildings and one closer shot where the different stages meet.
text.geographic_location: In the north part of Haugesund, with a view of the city park and rose garden.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, train or tram stops listed for this spot, so head for the city park and rose garden in the north part of Haugesund. From there, walk north-west to reach the building. The phone icon on the map is about 45 m south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole group of buildings in, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as where the old house meets the later extensions.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 45 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the vertical edges of the walls with them so the buildings do not lean. Try to include some of the park greenery at the edge of the frame. Then take a second shot using the telephoto to pick out the contrast between the older and newer parts.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the walls keep their detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime, when you can see the whole outside of the building clearly. A bright but cloudy day gives soft, even light on the walls.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the stand-here point, but check the official site before you go for opening arrangements and any rules on photography inside.
claims_not_in_sources: The park and rose garden area around the gallery can be walked through freely as public space.
Flowers in the rose garden may be usable as a foreground in the growing season.
Bright but cloudy light gives soft, even illumination on building walls.
Photography rules inside the gallery may be restricted, so visitors should check the official site.

text.description:
Dokken friluftsmuseum is an open-air museum in Haugesund, and the name tells you what to expect: buildings and objects shown outdoors rather than inside a gallery. That suits a phone camera well. You can usually step back, take in a whole building or scene, and then move in for details such as textures, doors and windows, or small objects. It is ranked third on the Haugesund map.

You don't need to hunt for an angle. Start there, take one wide frame to show the setting, then walk closer for a few tighter pictures. Turn on the gridlines in your camera settings so verticals such as walls and posts stay straight.

We have no details on the museum's history, buildings or opening arrangements, so check the official site before you go to see what is open and what can be photographed. If you go inside any building, ask before photographing people or displays.
text.geographic_location: In Haugesund, at the site known as Dokken.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot. Use the map to navigate to Dokken friluftsmuseum. The phone icon on the map is about 15 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the scene. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to a building and can't fit it all in. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 15 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Take one wide frame showing the whole scene, then a closer one on a detail. Switch on the gridlines and line up walls or posts with them so the picture does not lean. If the ultra-wide stretches the edges, keep the main subject towards the middle of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the subject to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is washing out. Try a Live Photo if there is movement, such as flags or people walking through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft daylight, in the morning or later in the afternoon, usually looks gentler than midday sun. Check opening arrangements first if you want to see the museum itself.

text.access_note: Access and opening arrangements are not confirmed here, so check the official site before you go.

name: Vår Frelsers Church
label: Vår Frelsers Church
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/107015337: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Vår Frelsers kirke' (53 m across).
notes: The main church of Haugesund, close to the town centre.

text.description: Vår Frelsers Church is a large red brick church in the middle of Haugesund. It was built in a Neo-gothic style and laid out as a cross, so the roofline has plenty of steep gables and pointed shapes. That makes it an easy subject for a phone: the dark red brick stands out against a pale sky, and the building is big enough to fill the frame from a distance. The architect was Einar Halleland, who won the design competition in February 1899. The church was built between 1899 and 1901 and consecrated on 6 March 1902. It seats about 850 people. Before it was built, people from the area went to the nearby Skåre Church. As Haugesund grew after becoming a town in 1854, residents asked for a church of their own in the centre. Start with a wide, straight-on view, then move in on the details: the pointed windows, the brickwork and the roof gables. If cars or people are in the way at street level, wait a moment or step a little to one side. Keep the phone level so the tall walls do not lean inwards.
text.geographic_location: The church stands in the centre of Haugesund, in the middle of the town.
text.directions_text: Start from the centre of Haugesund, where the church is easy to find. The phone icon on the map is about 85 m south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the whole church from where you stand. Switch to 2x or 3x telephoto for the gables and windows.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 85 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the church up so the walls stay straight. Keep a little sky above the roof so nothing is cut off. For a second shot, zoom in to 2x-3x and frame the cross-shaped gables and the pointed windows. Try the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you move closer, and keep the building centred so the edges do not stretch.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brickwork to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a touch if the sky is bright, so the red brick keeps its colour. Hold the phone with both hands and take two or three frames to be safe.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late afternoon light usually warms red brick nicely. On a grey day, the even light still works for a plain, clean record shot.

text.access_note: The church is a working parish church, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside, and dress respectfully.
claims_not_in_sources: Red brick usually looks warmer in soft morning or late afternoon light.
Visiting times and access to the inside may vary, so they should be checked with the parish.

name: Haugesund Teater
label: Haugesund Teater
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Haugesund Rådhus' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Haugesund rådhus' (way/38629165): middle (94 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q18887982: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: The historic theatre building near the harbour.

text.description:
Haugesund Teater is the regional theatre for Nord-Rogaland, set up in 1986. Its main stage is inside the Festiviteten culture house, so the building you photograph for the theatre is Festiviteten. The entrance side of Haugesund Rådhus (the town hall) is a spot where a historic photo of the newly built Festiviteten, held in the local museum collection, was taken. That makes it a sensible place for a phone photo with some local history behind it.

The building is a large, solid shape, so it works best as a simple, well-balanced picture. Dusk is the time to aim for, when the façade and the sky are both softly lit and the building stands out against the darker surroundings. The theatre also runs a smaller stage called HAUT on the Smedasundet waterfront. That is a separate place and not what you see from the town hall.

For a practical shot, go to the town hall entrance and look towards Festiviteten. Turn on the gridlines and keep the verticals straight by holding the phone upright. Leave a little space around the building rather than cutting it tight. If people or cars pass through the frame, wait a moment and take a few shots. A second option is the view from Risøybrua, which gives a wide panorama over Smedasundet and the town centre. The theatre may not be clearly visible from there, so treat it as a general town view.
text.geographic_location: In central Haugesund, with the theatre's main stage in the Festiviteten culture house. The theatre's HAUT stage is on the Smedasundet waterfront.
text.directions_text: From there the theatre is about 726 m to the north-west. Once you are at the town hall entrance, turn to look towards the Festiviteten building. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the whole building and a bit of its surroundings. Switch to 2x or 3x if your phone has a telephoto lens, to pick out the façade without moving. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a bold, close-up view, and keep the building well away from the edges, where it can look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Haugesund Rådhus (entrance side of the town hall, looking toward the Festiviteten building). The Festiviteten culture house, which holds the theatre's main stage, seen from the town hall entrance, especially at dusk. Looking towards the Festiviteten culture house, which holds the theatre's main stage. Check the framing when you arrive, as the exact view depends on where you stand.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the building up with the vertical lines so it does not lean. Leave some sky and foreground around it. If you want a second view, try Risøybrua for a wide panorama over Smedasundet and the town centre, though the theatre may be hard to pick out from there.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the façade to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little at dusk so the lit parts do not turn white. If the light is low, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body or rest the phone on a wall to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Dusk, when the building is lit against a darker sky.

text.access_note: You can photograph the outside from the town hall entrance side; for performances or going inside, check the official site before you go.

name: Skåre Church
label: Skåre Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Olav Kyrres gate' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Olav Kyrres gate nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/87393457: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Skåre kirke' (43 m across).
notes: Church in the northern part of Haugesund.

text.description:
Skåre Church is a white wooden church with an octagonal plan, built in 1858 to designs by the architect Christian Heinrich Grosch. It seats about 450 people. The site is much older than the building. Written records go back to 1301, and the first church here was a stave church that stood across the street from the present one. The church was built as the main church for the new town of Haugesund and its surroundings.

The view suggested here is a quieter one. From Olav Kyrres gate you look west along the street and see the church's east wall in the background, with the building at Erling Skjalgssons gate 15 on the right edge of the frame. You won't get the main facade from here. What you get is a plain white wall, a street scene and a sense of how the church sits among ordinary town buildings. That suits a phone well, because the white wall gives clean, simple shapes and the street leads the eye towards it.

The church is only a short stroll away, so it is easy to take a second shot from another side. Haugevegen gives a view from the east, with the villa at Haugevegen 17 on the left and the white Hauge skole building on the right. You can also walk the church grounds for a wider view of the whole octagonal church. Check on site that trees, parked cars or fences are not blocking the view.
text.geographic_location: Skåre Church stands in the town of Haugesund, with Olav Kyrres gate on its east side and Haugevegen nearby.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot. Head to Olav Kyrres gate in Haugesund, about 65 m east of the church. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which shows the church wall with some street around it. If the street is narrow or you want more of the building and sky, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x). Use telephoto (2x or more) for a tighter shot of the roofline and wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Olav Kyrres gate (looking west toward the church's east wall). The church's eastern wall in the background, with Erling Skjalgssons gate 15 on the right edge of the frame. The church's east wall is in the background, with Erling Skjalgssons gate 15 on the right edge of the frame. The church is to the west of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and use them to keep the walls and street edges straight. Let the street lead into the picture, with the white wall as the main subject and the building at number 15 as a frame on the right. If you want a different angle, Haugevegen gives a view of the church from the east, with the villa on the left and Hauge skole on the right.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the white wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so it stays white and keeps its detail rather than turning pale grey or washed out. Hold the phone level to avoid leaning walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning is likely to light the east wall, which faces you. In the late afternoon the sun is low in the west and behind the church, so the wall may look dark. Even, cloudy light also suits a white wall.

text.access_note: The street is public, but for access to the churchyard and any opening times, check the official site before you go.
